questions.stem: Which pesticide family targets unwanted plants growing among a crop?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Insecticides target insect pests.
Fungicides target fungal infections.
Bacteria are not the weeding target.

questions.stem: What immediate benefit do pesticides give a farmer?

options.text: Better flavour in the harvested produce
options.explanation: Flavour is not the mechanism.

options.text: A rapid reduction in pest numbers protecting the current crop
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A permanent end to all pest problems
options.explanation: Resistance and reapplication contradict that.

options.text: Fertilisation of the soil as a side effect
options.explanation: Pesticides kill pests; they do not feed the crop.

questions.stem: Why can insecticide use damage a crop's pollination?

options.explanation: Sterility is not the taught mechanism.
Repulsion is not how non-specific toxicity works.

options.text: Non-specific chemicals may kill bees and other pollinators visiting the crop
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Bees avoid any field with crops
options.explanation: Bees visit crops actively.

questions.stem: What does bioaccumulation threaten in an ecosystem?

options.explanation: Persistence harms predators, not fertility.
Residues do not feed the crop.
Resistance is an evolution outcome, not bioaccumulation.

options.text: Predators near the top of food chains gather harmful chemical concentrations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A farm has used the same insecticide for a decade and it now fails. What happened?

options.text: The pest population evolved resistance to the chemical
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Expiry dates are not the taught cause.
The crop is unchanged; the pest adapted.
Washing is loss, not failure of action.

questions.stem: State two advantages of using chemical pesticides on crops.
questions.modelAnswer: They act immediately and they are relatively cheap and accessible, killing the whole pest population present.

questions.stem: Name the three pesticide types matched to insects, weeds and fungi.
questions.modelAnswer: Insecticides kill insects, herbicides kill weeds, and fungicides kill fungal pests.

questions.stem: Explain why pesticides usually need to be applied repeatedly across a season.
questions.modelAnswer: New pests arrive or hatch after each application, and surviving resistant individuals breed, so one treatment never clears the population for long.

questions.stem: An orchard borders a beekeeper's hives. Recommend a control choice and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Avoid broad-spectrum insecticide sprays during flowering because non-specific chemicals would kill the pollinating bees, and choose a targeted or biological approach instead.

questions.stem: What does biological control use to suppress a pest species?

options.explanation: Barriers are exclusion, not biological control.

options.text: A natural predator or parasite introduced against it
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Chemicals define the other method.
Crop modification is not this technique.

questions.stem: Which pairing is a standard example of biological control in glasshouses?

options.explanation: Bees pollinate; they do not hunt fungus.
Netting is physical exclusion.

options.text: Parasitic wasps hunting whitefly on tomatoes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Ladybirds prey on aphids; they are not pollinators here.

questions.stem: Why does biological control leave some pests alive in the crop?

options.text: Predators refuse to hunt to completion
options.explanation: Cycle dynamics, not fussiness, keep prey present.
Hiding is not the mechanism described.
Established predators persist for long periods.

options.text: The predator-prey cycle stabilises the pest at low numbers instead of erasing it
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which disadvantage of biological control involves the introduced species itself?

options.text: It may fail to establish in the new area, or even become a pest
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It always mutates into a super-predator
options.explanation: Mutation claims are not part of the account.
Pollution is a chemical-control drawback.
Resistance concerns chemicals, not predators.

questions.stem: A grower needs pest suppression that lasts several seasons without respraying. Which method fits?

options.explanation: Glass is structural, not pest control.

options.text: Biological control, because its effect is long-lasting
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Chemicals need repeated application.
Herbicides target weeds, and still need reapplication.

questions.stem: State two advantages of biological control over chemical pesticides.
questions.modelAnswer: It causes no chemical pollution and the pest does not develop resistance, with effects lasting a long time.

questions.stem: Give the classic outdoor example of one insect eating another.
questions.modelAnswer: Ladybirds eat aphids, a natural predator-prey pairing used in biological control.

questions.stem: Explain why biological control can target a pest species specifically.
questions.modelAnswer: The introduced predator is chosen because it naturally attacks that pest, so the suppression falls on one species while most others go untouched.

questions.stem: Whitefly numbers rise in a tomato glasshouse. Outline the biological response and one monitoring step.
questions.modelAnswer: Introduce parasitic wasps to prey on the whitefly, then monitor leaves weekly to confirm the pest stays at low levels without chemical sprays.
